1359.title: Mirabai
1359.hook: messengers arrive at Dwarka to bring Mira home, and she asks for one more visit to the temple
1359.howItsDone: Pilgrims to Krishna's temple at Dwarka hear the story of Mira's last visit, and devotees remember her with her songs at Dwarka, in Vrindavan and in Rajasthan.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Mirabai and the stamp at the end of her songs: Mira's Lord is Giridhar.

A delegation from home stands at the door. They've traveled a long way, to a temple town by the sea on the far western coast. They've been sent to bring a woman back, and they aren't supposed to return without her. She listens. She doesn't say no. She asks for one thing first: let me go to the temple once more. The town is Dwarka, the city tradition gives to Krishna in his later life. The woman is Mira, and today, our last day with her, is the story tradition tells of how her road ended.
screen: `A DELEGATION AT THE DOOR.` → `DWARKA, BY THE SEA.` → `HOW HER ROAD ENDED.`

segments.voice: This is tradition's story, in paraphrase, not a record. After Vrindavan, Mira travels on to Dwarka, the city of Krishna as a king, where he is worshipped in the temple as Ranchhod, among other names. She sings there. Back in Mewar, things have gone badly, and some tellings say the royal house comes to believe its troubles began when Mira was driven out. So messengers are sent, some say priests among them, to bring her home. They plead; some tellings say they threaten to fast until she agrees. Mira asks only to go into the temple first, to take leave of her Lord. She goes in, and she doesn't come out. Tradition says she merged into the image of Krishna, and that her sari was found wrapped around it. Step back and look at her whole road in the songs and stories: the palace, the temple floor with bells on her feet, Vrindavan, Dwarka, and then into the shrine. Every step moves her closer to Krishna and further from what others had planned for her. Andal's story, a few days ago, ends almost the same way, with a woman going into a shrine and not coming out. Two women, two languages, far apart, and the tradition tells both endings as union, not death. And notice what Mira doesn't do. She doesn't refuse the messengers to their faces, or run. She asks for one last visit. In the story, that's all she needs.
screen: `MESSENGERS SENT TO DWARKA` · `ONE LAST VISIT TO THE TEMPLE` · `HER SARI AROUND THE IMAGE` · `A ROAD THAT ENDS IN UNION`

Notice the light, the sounds, what's on the walls, and stay a while; nobody is hurrying you. If you pray, you can take leave of that place with a word of thanks.

1360.title: Akka Mahadevi
1360.hook: a silkworm spins its own house from inside itself, and is caught in it: Akka Mahadevi's picture of desire
1360.howItsDone: Lingayats and other devotees of Shiva in Karnataka honor Akka Mahadevi among the vachana saints; her sayings are recited, sung and taught, and are read in Kannada and in translation.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Mirabai at Dwarka, asking for one last visit to the temple, and leaving only her sari behind. Today, a new voice from the south.

A silkworm doesn't find its house. It makes it, out of its own body, thread by thread, turning and turning, until the house is finished and the worm is sealed inside. Everything it needed came from within it, and so did the trap. That small, exact picture opens one of the sayings of a woman people called Akka, elder sister. She spoke to Shiva in Kannada, in the south, and her name for him was a flower.
screen: `A SILKWORM SPINS ITS HOUSE.` → `AKKA, ELDER SISTER.` → `HER NAME FOR GOD WAS A FLOWER.`

segments.voice: Her name is Mahadevi, and people called her Akka, elder sister, so she comes down to us as Akka Mahadevi. She belongs to the Virashaiva, or Lingayat, saints of Karnataka, devotees of Shiva who spoke their faith in short, sharp sayings called vachanas. They're not hymns for a temple choir. They're closer to speech, a person talking straight to God, or about God, in plain Kannada. Her sayings carry her name for Shiva: Chennamallikarjuna. Some readers render it as the beautiful lord, white as jasmine: a god called by the name of a small white flower. Now the silkworm, in paraphrase. The silkworm builds its house lovingly out of itself, and dies tangled in what it wound. So I burn with my heart's wanting. Lord white as jasmine, cut through this greed in me, and show me a way out. Notice first: she doesn't blame the world for trapping her. The thread comes from inside, her own wanting, spun round and round. That's honest, and it's uncomfortable. And she doesn't fix herself, either. She asks him to cut the thread. The way out, in the saying, is his doing, not her cleverness. Then listen to the voice. No priest stands between her and Shiva, no special language. A woman speaks in her own tongue, about her own heart, to a god she calls by the name of a flower. That directness is the gift of the vachanas, and Akka's voice is a sharp one.
screen: `AKKA, ELDER SISTER, SAINT OF SHIVA` · `THE LORD WHITE AS JASMINE` · `THE THREAD COMES FROM INSIDE` · `ASKING HIM TO CUT IT`

segments.voice: Notice one wanting active in you right now, maybe something small: a snack, a message, a result. Don't fight it or follow it; watch it spin the way you'd watch a silkworm turning, and on each out-breath loosen your grip a little. If you pray, you can ask, as Akka did, for help with the thread.
Akka Mahadevi. Elder sister, a saint of Shiva who spoke in Kannada vachanas, and called him the lord white as jasmine.
Your line: Akka Mahadevi. She didn't blame the world for the thread; she asked for it to be cut. Go gently.

1361.title: Akka Mahadevi
1361.hook: a woman arrives at a hall of saints with nothing but her hair, and the first thing she gets is a hard question
1361.howItsDone: Lingayat tradition tells Akka Mahadevi's arrival at Kalyana and her exchange with Allama Prabhu in its collections of the saints' dialogues, and her story is staged, sung and taught in Karnataka.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Akka Mahadevi, elder sister, and the silkworm caught in its own threads, asking the lord white as jasmine to cut them.

A gathering of saints in the city of Kalyana, where people come to talk about God plainly, and to be tested. In walks a young woman who has left a king's house. She has given up her clothes on the road; her long hair is all that covers her. Before she can sit, one of the saints, known for his searching questions, asks her something that would make anyone flinch. Her answer is what the story keeps. Today: the walk from the palace, and the test at the door.
screen: `A GATHERING OF SAINTS.` → `ONLY HER HAIR.` → `A QUESTION AT THE DOOR.`

segments.voice: Here's the story as her tradition tells it, in paraphrase. A local king, Kaushika, wants Mahadevi. The tellings differ on what happens next: some say she refuses him, some that she marries him on conditions he goes on to break. Either way, she leaves. Her vachanas speak of it plainly. Her husband, she says, is the lord white as jasmine, and she has no use for one who dies and decays. She walks away from the palace, sheds her clothes, and goes on, covered by her hair. On the road she comes to Kalyana, where the Virashaiva saints gather around Basavanna in a hall the tradition calls the Anubhava Mantapa, the hall of experience. There Allama Prabhu, a teacher famous in the stories for his hard questions, tests her. He asks, roughly: if you've truly given up the body's shame, why hide behind your hair? It's a fair question, and a cruel one, and she doesn't dodge it. Her answer comes in more than one form. In one, she says that until the fruit is ripe, the skin doesn't fall away. In another, that the covering is for the people looking, so the sight of her won't trouble them. Both answers refuse to pretend. She doesn't claim to be finished; she says she's ripening. And she thinks of the people around her, not only her own freedom. The saints don't send her away. Tradition says they welcome her, and call her Akka, elder sister. The test was the door, and she walked through it.
screen: `SHE LEAVES THE KING'S HOUSE` · `THE HALL OF EXPERIENCE` · `ALLAMA'S HARD QUESTION` · `UNTIL THE FRUIT IS RIPE`

segments.voice: Bring to mind one place in your life where you're not finished yet, a habit, a hurt, a hope, and without scolding it or pretending it's done, say quietly to yourself: still ripening. Breathe in and let it be unfinished; breathe out and let it grow in its own time. If you pray, you can offer the unripe part to God as it is.
Akka Mahadevi. She left a king for the lord white as jasmine, came to Kalyana in only her hair, and answered Allama's test: until the fruit is ripe, the skin stays on.

1362.title: Akka Mahadevi
1362.hook: a woman at a stranger's door, hands held out, asking God that nothing be put in them: Akka Mahadevi's strangest request
1362.tomorrow: Lal Ded — a season of the tradition's women
1362.howItsDone: In Karnataka, Akka Mahadevi is honored among the Lingayat (Virashaiva) saints, and her vachanas are sung, recited and taught in Kannada.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Akka Mahadevi in the hall at Kalyana, answering Allama's hard question: the skin falls away when the fruit is ripe.

A woman goes from house to house with her hands held out, a wandering seeker begging for her food. What's strange is what she asks for. She doesn't ask God to soften the hearts behind the doors. She asks for the doors to give her nothing. If they do give, she asks for the food to fall. And if it falls, something stranger still. Our last day with Akka Mahadevi: one short poem, and a request that runs backward.
screen: `HOUSE TO HOUSE, HANDS OUT.` → `SHE ASKS FOR NOTHING.` → `A REQUEST THAT RUNS BACKWARD.`

segments.voice: Here is the vachana, in paraphrase. Make me go from house to house, hands held out for alms. If I beg, let them give me nothing. If they give, let it fall to the ground. If it falls, before I can pick it up, let a dog come and take it, O lord white as jasmine. It works like a staircase going down. Each line takes away one more thing to lean on: the comfort of home, the kindness of strangers, the food already in her hand, even the chance to stoop and pick it up. At the bottom there's nothing left to hold, and the last words are his name. The poem doesn't end on the dog. It ends on the lord white as jasmine. Readers in her own tradition, the Lingayat or Virashaiva way of Karnataka, hear the stripping away of every support but one. Some readers also hear a sharp honesty: she knows how easily a full plate becomes the thing she trusts. So she asks to be emptied, all the way, until the only thing in her hands is him. The poem never says she starves, and it never asks anyone else to live this way. It's one woman, talking to the one she loves, about what she's willing to let go. And there's a small surprise at the bottom of the stairs. A hungry dog eats. Even her emptiness feeds someone. Three days with Akka: a silkworm caught in its own threads, a hard question at the door of the saints, and a woman asking for her hands to stay open.

1363.title: Lal Ded — a season of the tradition's women
1363.hook: a plate heaped with rice, and a stone hidden under it: the Kashmiri poet Lal Ded, and the one word her teacher gave her
1363.carry: Lal Ded — a season of the tradition's women
1363.tomorrow: Lal Ded — a season of the tradition's women
1363.howItsDone: Lal Ded's vakhs are recited and sung in Kashmiri, quoted in everyday speech, and remembered by Kashmiris of more than one faith.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Akka Mahadevi asked for her alms to fall and a dog to take them, and ended on the lord white as jasmine.

Dinner is served, and the young wife's plate looks generous, a full mound of rice. Only she knows what's underneath: a stone, with the rice spread thin over it, so the plate looks full while there's hardly anything to eat. Kashmiris tell this story about a young bride named Lalla and the mother-in-law who, tradition says, served her this way. She doesn't complain. She eats what there is, washes the stone, and sets it back. In time she would leave that house and become the poet Kashmir remembers as Lal Ded.
screen: `A FULL PLATE OF RICE.` → `A STONE UNDERNEATH.` → `THE BRIDE WHO BECAME LAL DED.`

segments.voice: She goes by more than one name: Lalla, Lalleshwari, and Lal Ded, the one Kashmir knows best. She sang in Kashmiri, not Sanskrit, in short sayings called vakhs, easy to remember and pass from mouth to mouth. The stories say that after years of hardship at home she walked out as a wandering seeker, and found a teacher. Then comes a saying about that teacher, in paraphrase. My teacher gave me only one word. He said: from outside, go within. That one word became my rule, and so I began to dance, with nothing on. Notice how little she was given. Not a library, not a long course of rituals. One word. And she didn't argue with it or add to it. She took it all the way. If what matters is within, then the outside, even the clothes, stops being the point. The stone story fits: a plate that looks full and isn't, and a bride who keeps quiet, because what feeds her isn't on the plate. Some readers hear her saying as a teaching about Shiva, found inside, the way some Shaiva teachers in Kashmir speak of him. Others hear a plainer lesson: a woman with almost nothing who turned that nothing into freedom. Year three gave a first glimpse of Lal Ded, searching far and finding at home. This season, four days with her, starting with the one word.
screen: `A POET OF MANY NAMES` · `SHORT SAYINGS IN KASHMIRI` · `ONE WORD: GO WITHIN` · `WHAT'S UNDER THE RICE`

If you pray, you can look for God there, within, in your own way.

1364.title: Lal Ded — a season of the tradition's women
1364.hook: a boat hauled across the sea on a rope of loose thread, and water seeping from an unbaked cup: Lal Ded admits she might not make it

1364.howItsDone: Lal Ded's vakhs, including this one, are recited and sung in Kashmiri, and Kashmiris quote her lines in everyday speech.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Lal Ded: the bride with a stone under her rice, and the one word her teacher gave her, from outside, go within.

A cup shaped from wet clay and dried in the sun, but never fired in a kiln. It looks like a cup. It holds its shape. Pour water in, though, and the sides darken. Drop by drop, the water soaks into the clay and seeps away, and the cup begins to soften. In one saying Lal Ded uses that kind of cup to describe herself, next to an even shakier picture: a boat, a whole sea, and a rope of loose thread.
screen: `A CUP OF UNBAKED CLAY.` → `THE WATER SEEPS AWAY.` → `A BOAT ON A ROPE OF THREAD.`

segments.voice: Here is the vakh, in paraphrase. With a rope of loose, untwisted thread, I am hauling a boat across the sea. If only God would hear me and carry me over. Like water in cups of unbaked clay, I am seeping away. How I long to go home. Take the pictures one at a time. First the rope. A boat on the open sea is heavy, and the water pulls against it; towing it with untwisted thread is close to hopeless. The rope is whatever she has to pull with: her effort, her discipline, her practice. She doesn't pretend it's strong. Then the prayer in the middle: if only God would hear me. She isn't boasting that she's arrived. She's asking to be carried. Then the cup, her life draining away a little each day, the way water leaves unfired clay. Then the last word, home. Not the house she left. Some Shaiva readers in Kashmir hear the self finding its way back to Shiva, its true home; some hear, more simply, the ache to be where you belong. Notice the honesty. The woman who danced free on one word, remembered as a teacher, says plainly: my rope is weak, my time is leaking, I may not make it across on my own. The tradition kept this saying. It didn't polish it into a victory. It let a saint say she was struggling.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Lal Ded hauled a boat with a rope of loose thread, seeping away like water in unbaked clay, and still longed for home.

A length of cloth, torn into two equal strips, one over each shoulder. That's how one Kashmiri story has Lal Ded walking through town. Every time someone mocks her, she ties a knot in one strip. Every time someone bows and praises her, she ties a knot in the other. By evening both are full of knots. Then, the story says, she has them weighed. They weigh exactly the same. It's a story told about her, not one she told. But she has a saying that sounds just like it.
screen: `TWO STRIPS OF CLOTH.` → `A KNOT FOR EACH INSULT, A KNOT FOR EACH BOW.` → `THEY WEIGH THE SAME.`

segments.voice: Here is the vakh, in paraphrase. Let them curse me, let them jeer at me. Let each one say whatever pleases them. Let the good come and worship me with flowers. What does any of it gain them? I remain untouched. The first time through, it can sound cold, as if she doesn't care about anyone. Look again. She isn't telling the mockers to stop, and she isn't refusing the flowers. She lets both come. What she won't do is let either one decide who she is. The insult doesn't shrink her. The garland doesn't swell her. That's the knot story in a few lines: praise and blame, on the same scale, weigh the same. This was no small thing for a woman who had left her husband's house and walked about as a wandering seeker; tradition says she drew plenty of both. The Bhagavad Gita, describing the one dear to Krishna, speaks of someone the same in honor and dishonor, with friend and foe. Lal Ded's saying lives in that neighborhood, in her own Kashmiri words, about her own street. And the week looks back: Mirabai, then three days with Akka Mahadevi, and three with Lal Ded: one word, go within; a rope of loose thread; two strips of cloth that weigh the same. Different languages, different corners of India, each woman in words of her own.
